source: Technology Promotion Project to Increase Productivity Around Tonle Sap (TSTD — TA 7305-CAM), watermelon (ដំណាំឪឡឹក) technical training booklet, prepared by the project's agricultural techniques and extension officer in cooperation with East West Seed International, November 2016. Contact: livleanghy@gmail.com
text:
The booklet stresses that recording production costs and income is very important for farmers, and notes that many farmers fail to keep such records. Without a record of what was spent and earned, a farmer cannot actually tell whether the crop made a loss or a profit — receiving cash from a sale on a given day does not by itself mean the farmer is profiting overall.

Keeping records lets a farmer see which cost items and which income items are out of balance, so avoidable costs can be identified and spending can be managed better going forward. Records from past seasons also help farmers plan and budget for future production, since they show what things actually cost and what the crop actually returned.

The core idea presented: profit is the difference between the income earned from production (such as selling the fruit) and the total cost of production. Total cost of production is the sum of variable costs (costs that change with output or activity, such as transport cost for a longer delivery distance) and fixed costs (costs that do not change over the period, such as land or equipment costs already committed).

To support this, the booklet provides blank record-keeping tables for a farmer to fill in: a cost table (item, unit, quantity, unit price, total cost, notes) and a revenue/income table (item, unit, quantity, unit price, total income, notes), plus a combined cost-revenue-profit worksheet for one growing cycle. That worksheet separates variable costs (TVC) — such as land preparation, seed, fertilizer, pesticide, and paid labor — from fixed costs (TFC) — such as land rent, tools, and unpaid family labor — sums them into total cost (TC = TVC + TFC), and then calculates cost per kilogram of yield (TC divided by total yield) and profit per kilogram (net profit divided by total yield), where net profit is total income minus total cost.
